title: A year without meat
hookLine: Seneca tried his teacher Sotion's diet for a year and felt clearer, then stopped for political reasons (Letters 108)

lines: THE EXPERIMENT IN YOUR NOTES APP.
A YOUNG MAN CHANGES HIS PLATE.
THEN STOPS, FOR AN ODD REASON.
cards: Somewhere in your phone there's probably a note about an experiment you meant to run on yourself. Thirty days without sugar. A month off social media.
Waking at six. Notes like that can sit there for years. In Letter 108, Seneca confesses one experiment he actually ran.

As a young man in Rome, he was so taken with what his teacher said that he changed what he put on his plate, and kept it up for a full year. Then he stopped, and the reason isn't the one you'd expect.

teach.h: SOTION: TWO REASONS, NO LOSS EITHER WAY.
teach.b: First, the teacher. Sotion gave his students two reasons for not eating animals. Pythagoras' reason: souls pass from body to body, so the animal on your plate may house a soul like yours.
And the reason of another teacher, Sextius: there's food enough without bloodshed, and a habit of cruelty, once practiced at the table, spreads. Sotion added a shrewd twist.
If Pythagoras is right, abstaining spares you a wrong. If he's wrong, abstaining is simple living. Either way you lose nothing.

teach.h: A YEAR, EASY AND THEN PLEASANT.
teach.b: Within a year, Seneca says, the habit was not only easy but pleasant.
He thought his mind felt quicker, then adds, honestly, that he couldn't swear today whether it really was. Third, why he stopped.
Early in the emperor Tiberius' reign, foreign religions were being driven out of Rome, and refusing certain meats could be read as a sign you belonged to one.

His father, who, Seneca says, wasn't afraid of being accused of anything but did dislike philosophy, asked him to eat like everyone else. It wasn't hard, Seneca admits, to persuade him to dine better.
Fourth, what the letter is about. Not a diet.
Seneca was the kind of student who tried things: he heard a teacher, and his life moved.
Some traditions keep a meatless table and others don't; this letter doesn't settle that. It tells a story about taking an idea seriously enough to test it.

how: Some readers of the Stoics run small, time-limited experiments in simpler living, such as a plainer diet for a set period, and notice honestly what changes, the way Seneca describes in Letter 108.

o: the emperor who drove foreign cults from Rome
a teacher whose diet young Seneca tried for a year
the Greek thinker who taught that souls move on

games.q: a year without meat — tap the pairs.
p: souls pass from body to body
disliked philosophy, asked him to stop

s: Seneca stopped because the diet made him ill
he stopped when abstaining could look like belonging to a banned foreign cult, and his father asked him to.
Seneca admits he can't be sure his mind really was quicker
he says he thought so, but wouldn't swear to it now.

the letter tells his story; it isn't a rule for readers.

games.q: you're young Seneca. you've kept your teacher's diet for a year and like it. rumors start about foreign cults. your father asks you to stop. what do you do?
games.why: he went back to eating like everyone else, and admits with a smile it wasn't hard to persuade him.

practice: Take one bite of something now if you have food with you, or picture your last meal, and eat it the way someone in the middle of an experiment would: paying attention.
Notice where it came from, the first taste, and how fast the second bite wants to follow. Put the fork down between bites, even in your imagination.

wordCard.voice: Sotion. The teacher whose vegetarian reasoning young Seneca tested on his own plate for a year, easy, then pleasant, then stopped at his father's request. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, the later name for Pythagoras' teaching that souls pass from body to body.

carryVoice: Your line: try it. An idea taken seriously is an idea tested. That's day four hundred eighty-five.
